entries.2ff9d5cd2c314569a4e3d7967499e32a4b960b93: <div sID="gen17846" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="30" osisID="Jer.30" sID="Jer.30"/> <div eID="gen17846" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17847" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17848" type="x-p"/> The sermon which we have in this and the following chapter is of a very different complexion from all those before. The prophet does indeed, by direction from God, change his voice. Most of what he had said hitherto was by way of reproof and threatening; but these two chapters are wholly taken up with precious promises of a return out of captivity, and that typical of the glorious things reserved for the church in the days of the Messiah. The prophet is told not only to preach this, but to write it, because it is intended for the comfort of the generation to come, <reference osisRef="Jer.30.1-Jer.30.3">ver. 1-3</reference>. It is here promised, I. That they should hereafter have a joyful restoration. 1. Though they were now in a great deal of pain and terror, <reference osisRef="Jer.30.4-Jer.30.7">ver. 4-7</reference>. 2. Though their oppressors were very strong, <reference osisRef="Jer.30.8-Jer.30.10">ver. 8-10</reference>. 3. Though a full end was made of other nations, and they were not restored, <reference osisRef="Jer.30.11">ver. 11</reference>. 4. Though all means of their deliverance seemed to fail and be cut off, <reference osisRef="Jer.30.12-Jer.30.14">ver. 12-14</reference>. 5. Though God himself had sent them into captivity, and justly, for their sins, <reference osisRef="Jer.30.15-Jer.30.16">ver. 15, 16</reference>. 6. Though all about them looked upon their case as desperate, <reference osisRef="Jer.30.17">ver. 17</reference>. II. That after their joyful restoration they should have a happy settlement, that their city should be rebuilt (<reference osisRef="Jer.30.18">ver. 18</reference>), their numbers increased (<reference osisRef="Jer.30.19">ver. 19, 20</reference>), their government established (<reference osisRef="Jer.30.21">ver. 21</reference>), God's covenant with them renewed (<reference osisRef="Jer.30.22">ver. 22</reference>), and their enemies destroyed and cut off, <reference osisRef="Jer.30.23-Jer.30.24">ver. 23, 24</reference>.
entries.3fb4922217330b665b4c01725aa403161bab6665: <div eID="gen17848" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17847" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Promises of Mercy. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 594.)</title> <div sID="gen17849" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The word that came to Jeremiah from the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , saying, <hi type="super">2</hi> Thus speaketh the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of Israel, saying, Write thee all the words that I have spoken unto thee in a book. <hi type="super">3</hi> For, lo, the days come, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , that I will bring again the captivity of my people Israel and Judah, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : and I will cause them to return to the land that I gave to their fathers, and they shall possess it. <hi type="super">4</hi> And these <hi type="italic">are</hi> the words that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spake concerning Israel and concerning Judah. <hi type="super">5</hi> For thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; We have heard a voice of trembling, of fear, and not of peace. <hi type="super">6</hi> Ask ye now, and see whether a man doth travail with child? wherefore do I see every man with his hands on his loins, as a woman in travail, and all faces are turned into paleness? <hi type="super">7</hi> Alas! for that day <hi type="italic">is</hi> great, so that none <hi type="italic">is</hi> like it: it <hi type="italic">is</hi> even the time of Jacob's trouble; but he shall be saved out of it. <hi type="super">8</hi> For it shall come to pass in that day, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, <hi type="italic">that</hi> I will break his yoke from off thy neck, and will burst thy bonds, and strangers shall no more serve themselves of him: <hi type="super">9</hi> But they shall serve the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> their God, and David their king, whom I will raise up unto them. <div eID="gen17849" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17850" type="x-p"/> Here, I. Jeremiah is directed to <hi type="italic">write</hi> what God had spoken to him, which perhaps refers to all the foregoing prophecies. He must write them and publish them, in hopes that those who had not profited by what he said upon once hearing it might take more notice of it when in reading it they had leisure for a more considerate review. Or, rather, it refers to the promises of their enlargement, which had been often mixed with his other discourses. He must collect them and put them together, and God will now add unto them many like words. He must write them for the generations to come, who should see them accomplished, and thereby have their faith in the prophecy confirmed. He must write them not <hi type="italic">in a letter,</hi> as that in the chapter before to the captives, but <hi type="italic">in a book,</hi> to be carefully preserved in the archives, or among the public rolls or registers of the state. Daniel understood by these books when the captivity was about coming to an end, <reference osisRef="Dan.9.2">Dan. ix. 2</reference>. He must write them in a book, not in loose papers: "<hi type="italic">For the days come,</hi> and are yet at a great distance, when <hi type="italic">I will bring again the captivity of Israel and Judah,</hi> great numbers of the ten tribes, with those of the two," <reference osisRef="Jer.30.3">v. 3</reference>. And this prophecy must be written, that it may be read then also, that so it may appear how exactly the accomplishment answers the prediction, which is one end of the writing of prophecies. It is intimated that they shall be <hi type="italic">beloved for their fathers' sake</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.28">Rom. xi. 28</reference>); for <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> God will bring them again to Canaan, because it was <hi type="italic">the land that he gave to their fathers,</hi> which therefore <hi type="italic">they shall possess.</hi> <div eID="gen17850" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17851" type="x-p"/> II. He is directed what to write. The very words are such as the Holy Ghost teaches, <reference osisRef="Jer.30.4">v. 4</reference>. These are the words which God ordered to be written; and those promises which are written by his order are as truly his word as the ten commandments which were written with his finger. 1. He must write a description of the fright and consternation which the people were now in, and were likely to be still in upon every attack that the Chaldeans made upon them, which will much magnify both the wonder and the welcomeness of their deliverance (<reference osisRef="Jer.30.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">We have heard a voice of trembling</hi>—the shrieks of terror echoing to the alarms of danger. The false prophets told them that they should have <hi type="italic">peace,</hi> but <hi type="italic">there is fear and not peace,</hi> so the margin reads it. No marvel that when <hi type="italic">without are fightings within are fears.</hi> The men, even the men of war, shall be quite overwhelmed with the calamities of their nation, shall sink under them, and yield to them, and shall look like <hi type="italic">women in labour,</hi> whose pains come upon them in great extremity and they know that they cannot escape them, <reference osisRef="Jer.30.6">v. 6</reference>. You never heard of a man travailing with child, and yet here you find not here and there a timorous man, but <hi type="italic">every man with his hands on his loins,</hi> in the utmost anguish and agony, <hi type="italic">as women in travail,</hi> when they see their cities burnt and their countries laid waste. But this pain is compared to that of a woman in travail, not to that of a death-bed, because it shall end in joy at last, and the pain, like that of a travailing woman, shall be forgotten. <hi type="italic">All faces</hi> shall be <hi type="italic">turned into paleness.</hi> The word signifies not only such paleness as arises from a sudden fright, but that which is the effect of a bad habit of body, the jaundice, or the green sickness. The prophet laments the calamity upon the foresight of it (<reference osisRef="Jer.30.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">Alas! for that day is great,</hi> a day of judgment, which is called the <hi type="italic">great day,</hi> the <hi type="italic">great and terrible day of the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Joel.2.31">Joel ii. 31</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jude.1.6">Jude 6</reference>), great, so that <hi type="italic">there has been none like it.</hi> The last destruction of Jerusalem is thus spoken of by our Saviour as unparalleled, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.21">Matt. xxiv. 21</reference>. <hi type="italic">It is even the time of Jacob's trouble,</hi> a sad time, when God's professing people shall be in distress above other people. The whole time of the captivity was a time of Jacob's trouble; and such times ought to be greatly lamented by all that are concerned for the welfare of Jacob and the honour of the God of Jacob. 2. He must write the assurances which God had given that a happy end should at length be put to these calamities. (1.) Jacob's troubles shall cease: <hi type="italic">He shall be saved out of them.</hi> Though the afflictions of the church may last long, they shall not last always. <hi type="italic">Salvation belongs to the Lord,</hi> and shall be wrought for his church. (2.) Jacob's troublers shall be disabled from doing him any further mischief, and shall be reckoned with for the mischief they have done him, <reference osisRef="Jer.30.8">v. 8</reference>. <hi type="italic">The Lord of hosts,</hi> who has all power in his hand, undertakes to do it: "<hi type="italic">I will break his yoke from off thy neck,</hi> which has long lain so heavy, and has so sorely galled thee. <hi type="italic">I will burst thy bonds</hi> and restore thee to liberty and ease, and thou shalt no more be at the beck and command of strangers, shalt no more serve them, nor shall they any more <hi type="italic">serve themselves of thee;</hi> they shall no more enrich themselves either by thy possessions or by thy labours." And, (3.) That which crowns and completes the mercy is that they shall be restored to the free exercise of their religion again, <reference osisRef="Jer.30.9">v. 9</reference>. They shall be delivered from serving their enemies, not that they may live at large and do what they please, but that they may <hi type="italic">serve the Lord their God and David their king,</hi> that they may come again into order, under the established government both in church and state. <hi type="italic">Therefore</hi> they were brought into trouble and made to <hi type="italic">serve their enemies</hi> because they had not <hi type="italic">served the Lord their God</hi> as they ought to have done, <hi type="italic">with joyfulness and gladness of heart,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.28.47">Deut. xxviii. 47</reference>. But, when the time shall come that they should be <hi type="italic">saved out of their trouble,</hi> God will prepare and qualify them for it by giving them a <hi type="italic">heart to serve him,</hi> and will make it doubly comfortable by giving them opportunity to serve him. <hi type="italic">Therefore</hi> we are <hi type="italic">delivered out of the hands of our enemies,</hi> that we may <hi type="italic">serve God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.1.74-Luke.1.75">Luke i. 74, 75</reference>. And <hi type="italic">then</hi> deliverances out of temporal calamities are mercies indeed to us when by them we find ourselves engaged to and enlarged in the service of God. They shall serve their own God, and neither be inclined, as they had been of old in the day of their apostasy, nor compelled, as they had been of late in the day of their captivity, to serve other gods. They shall serve <hi type="italic">David their king,</hi> such governors as God should from time to time set over them, of the line of David (as Zerubbabel), or at least sitting on the <hi type="italic">thrones of judgment, the thrones of the house of David,</hi> as Nehemiah. But certainly this has a further meaning. The Chaldee paraphrase reads it, <hi type="italic">They shall obey</hi> (or <hi type="italic">hearken to</hi>) <hi type="italic">the Messiah</hi> (or <hi type="italic">Christ</hi>), the <hi type="italic">Son of David, their king.</hi> To him the Jewish interpreters apply it. That dispensation which commenced at their return out of captivity brought them to the Messiah. He is called <hi type="italic">David their King</hi> because he was the <hi type="italic">Son of David</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.22.42">Matt. xxii. 42</reference>) and he answered to the name, <reference osisRef="Matt.20.31-Matt.20.32">Matt. xx. 31, 32</reference>. David was an illustrious type of him both in his humiliation and in his exaltation. The covenant of royalty made with David had principal reference to him, and in him the promises of that covenant had their full accomplishment. God gave him the <hi type="italic">throne of his father David;</hi> he <hi type="italic">raised him up unto them, set him upon the holy hill of Zion.</hi> God is often in the New Testament said to have <hi type="italic">raised up Jesus,</hi> raised him up as a King, <reference osisRef="Acts.3.26">Acts iii. 26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.13.23 Acts.13.33">xiii. 23, 33</reference>. Observe, [1.] Those that serve the Lord as their God must also serve <hi type="italic">David their King,</hi> must give up themselves to Jesus Christ, to be ruled by him. For all men must <hi type="italic">honour the Son as they honour the Father,</hi> and come into the service and worship of God by him as Mediator. [2.] Those that are delivered out of spiritual bondage must make it appear that they are so by giving up themselves to the service of Christ. Those to whom he gives rest must take his yoke upon them.
entries.431d1b31b6fcd2962c179916f8c5f844ed810871: <div eID="gen17851" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Promises of Mercy. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 594.)</title> <div sID="gen17852" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> Therefore fear thou not, O my servant Jacob, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; neither be dismayed, O Israel: for, lo, I will save thee from afar, and thy seed from the land of their captivity; and Jacob shall return, and shall be in rest, and be quiet, and none shall make <hi type="italic">him</hi> afraid. <hi type="super">11</hi> For I <hi type="italic">am</hi> with thee, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , to save thee: though I make a full end of all nations whither I have scattered thee, yet will I not make a full end of thee: but I will correct thee in measure, and will not leave thee altogether unpunished. <hi type="super">12</hi> For thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , Thy bruise <hi type="italic">is</hi> incurable, <hi type="italic">and</hi> thy wound <hi type="italic">is</hi> grievous.   13 <hi type="italic">There is</hi> none to plead thy cause, that thou mayest be bound up: thou hast no healing medicines. <hi type="super">14</hi> All thy lovers have forgotten thee; they seek thee not; for I have wounded thee with the wound of an enemy, with the chastisement of a cruel one, for the multitude of thine iniquity; <hi type="italic">because</hi> thy sins were increased. <hi type="super">15</hi> Why criest thou for thine affliction? thy sorrow <hi type="italic">is</hi> incurable for the multitude of thine iniquity: <hi type="italic">because</hi> thy sins were increased, I have done these things unto thee. <hi type="super">16</hi> Therefore all they that devour thee shall be devoured; and all thine adversaries, every one of them, shall go into captivity; and they that spoil thee shall be a spoil, and all that prey upon thee will I give for a prey. <hi type="super">17</hi> For I will restore health unto thee, and I will heal thee of thy wounds, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; because they called thee an Outcast, <hi type="italic">saying,</hi> This <hi type="italic">is</hi> Zion, whom no man seeketh after. <div eID="gen17852" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17853" type="x-p"/> In these verses, as in those foregoing, the deplorable case of the Jews in captivity is set forth, but many precious promises are given them that in due time they should be relieved and a glorious salvation wrought for them. <div eID="gen17853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17854" type="x-p"/> I. God himself appeared against them: he <hi type="italic">scattered</hi> them (<reference osisRef="Jer.30.11">v. 11</reference>); he did <hi type="italic">all these things unto them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.30.15">v. 15</reference>. All their calamities came from his hands; whoever were the instruments, he was the principal agent. And this made their case very sad that God, even their own God, spoke concerning them, to pull down and to destroy. Now, 1. This was intended by him as a fatherly chastisement, and no other (<reference osisRef="Jer.30.11">v. 11</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I will correct thee in measure,</hi> or <hi type="italic">according to judgment,</hi> with discretion, no more than thou deservest, nay, no more than thou canst well bear." What God does against his people is in a way of correction, and that correction is always moderated and always proceeds from love: "<hi type="italic">I will not leave thee altogether unpunished,</hi> as thou art ready to think I should, because of thy relation to me." Note, A profession of religion, though ever so plausible, will be far from securing to us impunity in sin. God is no respecter of persons, but will show his hatred of sin wherever he finds it, and that he hates it most in those that are nearest to him. God here corrects his people <hi type="italic">for the multitude of their iniquity,</hi> and <hi type="italic">because their sins were increased,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.30.14-Jer.30.15">v. 14, 15</reference>. Are our sorrows multiplied at any time and do they increase? We must acknowledge that it is because our sins have been multiplied and they have increased. Iniquities grow in us, and therefore troubles grow upon us. But, 2. What God intended as a fatherly chastisement they and others interpreted as an act of hostility; they looked upon him as having <hi type="italic">wounded them with the wound of an enemy</hi> and <hi type="italic">with the chastisement of a cruel one</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.30.14">v. 14</reference>), as if he had designed their ruin, and neither mitigated the correction nor had any mercy in reserve for them. It did indeed seem as if God had dealt thus severely with them, as if he had turned to be their enemy and had fought against them, <reference osisRef="Isa.63.10">Isa. lxiii. 10</reference>. Job complains that God had become cruel to him and <hi type="italic">multiplied his wounds.</hi> When troubles are great and long we have need carefully to watch over our own hearts, that we entertain not such hard thoughts as these of God and his providence. His are the chastisements of a merciful one, not of a cruel one, whatever they may appear. <div eID="gen17854" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17855" type="x-p"/> II. Their friends forsook them, and were shy of them. None of those who had courted them in their prosperity would take notice of them now in their distress, <reference osisRef="Jer.30.13">v. 13</reference>. It is commonly thus when families go to decay; those hang off from them that had been their hangers-on. In two cases we are glad of the assistance of our friends and need their service:—1. If we be impeached, accused, or reproached, we expect that our friends should appear in vindication of us, should speak a good word for us when we cannot put on a face to speak for ourselves; but here <hi type="italic">there is none to plead thy cause,</hi> none to stand up in thy defence, none to intercede for thee with thy oppressors; therefore God will <hi type="italic">plead their cause,</hi> for he might well wonder there was none to uphold a people that had been so much the favourites of Heaven, <reference osisRef="Isa.63.5">Isa. lxiii. 5</reference>. 2. If we be sick, or sore, or wounded, we expect our friends should attend us, advise us, sympathize with us, and, if occasion be, lend a hand for the applying of healing medicines; but here there is none to do that, none to bind up thy wounds, and by counsels and comforts to make proper applications to thy case; nay (<reference osisRef="Jer.30.14">v. 14</reference>), <hi type="italic">All thy lovers have forgotten thee;</hi> out of sight out of mind; instead of seeking thee, they forsake thee. Such as this has often been the case of religion and serious godliness in the world; those that from their education, profession, and hopeful beginnings, one might have expected to be its friends and lovers, its patrons and protectors, desert it, forget it, and have nothing to say in its defence, nor will do any thing towards the healing of its wounds. Observe, <hi type="italic">Thy lovers have forgotten thee, for I have wounded thee.</hi> When God is against a people who will be for them? Who can be for them so as to do them any kindness? See <reference osisRef="Job.30.11">Job xxx. 11</reference>. Now, upon this account, their case seemed desperate and past relief (<reference osisRef="Jer.30.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thy bruise is incurable, thy wound grievous,</hi> and (<reference osisRef="Jer.30.15">v. 15</reference>) <hi type="italic">thy sorrow is incurable.</hi> The condition of the Jews in captivity was such as no human power could redress the grievances of; there they were like a valley full of <hi type="italic">dead and dry bones,</hi> which nothing less than Omnipotence can put life into. Who could imagine that a people so diminished, so impoverished, should ever be restored to their own land and re-established there? So many were the aggravations of their calamity that their sorrow would not admit of any alleviation, but they seemed to be hardened in it, and their souls refused to be comforted, till divine consolations proved strong ones, too strong to be borne down even by the floods of grief that overwhelmed them. <hi type="italic">Thy sorrow is incurable because thy sins,</hi> instead of being repented of and forsaken, <hi type="italic">were increased.</hi> Note, Incurable griefs are owing to incurable lusts. Now in this deplorable condition they are looked upon with disdain (<reference osisRef="Jer.30.17">v. 17</reference>): <hi type="italic">They called thee an outcast,</hi> abandoned by all, abandoned to ruin; they said, <hi type="italic">This is Zion, whom no man seeks after.</hi> When they looked on the place where the city and temple had been built they called that an outcast; now all was in ruins, there was no resort to it, no residence in it, none asked the way to Zion, as formerly; <hi type="italic">no man seeks after</hi> it. When they looked on the people that formerly dwelt in Zion, but were now in captivity (and we read of <hi type="italic">Zion dwelling with the daughter of Babylon,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.2.7">Zech. ii. 7</reference>), they called them outcasts; these are those who belong to Zion, and are wont to talk much of it and weep at the remembrance of it, but <hi type="italic">no man seeks after</hi> them, or enquires concerning them. Note, It is often the lot of Zion to be deserted and despised by those about her. <div eID="gen17855" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17856" type="x-p"/> III. For all this God will work deliverance and salvation for them in due time. Though no other hand, nay, <hi type="italic">because</hi> no other hand, can cure their wound, his will, and shall. 1. Though he seemed to stand at a distance from them, yet he assures them of his presence with them, his powerful and gracious presence: <hi type="italic">I will save thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.30.10">v. 10</reference>. <hi type="italic">I am with thee, to save thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.30.11">v. 11</reference>. When they are in their troubles he is with them, to save them from sinking under them; when the time has come for their deliverance he is with them, to be ready upon the first opportunity, to save them out of their trouble. 2. Though they were at a distance, remote from their own land, <hi type="italic">afar</hi> off <hi type="italic">in the land of their captivity,</hi> yet there shall salvation find them out, thence shall it fetch them, them and their <hi type="italic">seed,</hi> for they also shall be known among the Gentiles, and distinguished from them, that they may <hi type="italic">return,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.30.10">v. 10</reference>. 3. Though they were now full of fears, and continually alarmed, yet the time shall come when they <hi type="italic">shall be in rest and quiet,</hi> safe and easy, <hi type="italic">and none shall make them afraid,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.30.10">v. 10</reference>. 4. Though the nations into which they were dispersed should be brought to ruin, yet they should be preserved from that ruin (<reference osisRef="Jer.30.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">Though I make a full end of the nations whither I have scattered thee,</hi> and there might be danger of thy being lost among them, <hi type="italic">yet I will not make a full end of thee.</hi> It was promised that in the peace of these nations they should <hi type="italic">have peace</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.29.7">ch. xxix. 7</reference>), and yet in the destruction of these nations they should escape destruction. God's church may sometimes be brought very low, but he <hi type="italic">will not make a full end of</hi> it, <reference osisRef="Jer.5.10">ch. v. 10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.5.18">18</reference>. 5. Though God correct them, and justly, for their sins, their manifold transgressions and mighty sins, yet he will return in mercy to them, and even their sin shall not prevent their deliverance when God's time shall come. 6. Though their adversaries were mighty, God will bring them down, and break their power (<reference osisRef="Jer.30.16">v. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">All that devour thee shall be devoured,</hi> and thus Zion's cause will be pleaded and will be made to appear to all the world a righteous cause. Thus Zion's deliverance will be brought about by the destruction of her oppressors; and thus her enemies will be recompensed for all the injury they have done her; for <hi type="italic">there is a God that judges in the earth,</hi> a God <hi type="italic">to whom vengeance belongs.</hi> "They <hi type="italic">shall every one of them,</hi> without exception, <hi type="italic">go into captivity,</hi> and the day will come when <hi type="italic">those that</hi> now <hi type="italic">spoil thee shall be a spoil.</hi>" Those that <hi type="italic">lead into captivity shall go into captivity,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.13.10">Rev. xiii. 10</reference>. This might serve to oblige the present conquerors to use their captives well, because the wheel would turn round, and the day would come when they also should be captives, and let them do now as they would then be done by. 7. Though the wound seem incurable, God will make a cure of it (<reference osisRef="Jer.30.17">v. 17</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will restore health unto thee.</hi> Be the disease ever so dangerous, the patient is safe if God undertakes the cure. <div eID="gen17856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17857" type="x-p"/> IV. Upon the whole matter, they are cautioned against inordinate fear and grief, for in these precious promises there is enough to silence both. 1. They must not tremble as those that have no hope in the apprehension of future further trouble that might threaten them (<reference osisRef="Jer.30.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">Fear thou not, O my servant Jacob! neither be dismayed.</hi> Note, Those that are God's servants must not give way to disquieting fears, whatever difficulties and dangers may be before them. 2. They must not sorrow as those that have no hope for the troubles which at present they lie under, <reference osisRef="Jer.30.15">v. 15</reference>. "<hi type="italic">Why criest thou for thy affliction?</hi> It is true thy carnal confidences fail thee, creatures are physicians of no value, but <hi type="italic">I will heal thy wound,</hi> and therefore, <hi type="italic">Why criest thou?</hi> Why dost thou fret and complain thus? It is <hi type="italic">for thy sin</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.30.14-Jer.30.15">v. 14, 15</reference>), and therefore, instead of repining, thou shouldest be repenting. <hi type="italic">Wherefore should a man complain for the punishment of his sins?</hi> The issue will be good at last, and therefore <hi type="italic">rejoice in hope.</hi>"
entries.68137c2c8dac534b595982971b57c6994f382ce9: <div eID="gen17857" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Promises of Mercy. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 594.)</title> <div sID="gen17858" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; Behold, I will bring again the captivity of Jacob's tents, and have mercy on his dwelling-places; and the city shall be builded upon her own heap, and the palace shall remain after the manner thereof. <hi type="super">19</hi> And out of them shall proceed thanksgiving and the voice of them that make merry: and I will multiply them, and they shall not be few; I will also glorify them, and they shall not be small. <hi type="super">20</hi> Their children also shall be as aforetime, and their congregation shall be established before me, and I will punish all that oppress them. <hi type="super">21</hi> And their nobles shall be of themselves, and their governor shall proceed from the midst of them; and I will cause him to draw near, and he shall approach unto me: for who <hi type="italic">is</hi> this that engaged his heart to approach unto me? saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">22</hi> And ye shall be my people, and I will be your God. <hi type="super">23</hi> Behold, the whirlwind of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> goeth forth with fury, a continuing whirlwind: it shall fall with pain upon the head of the wicked. <hi type="super">24</hi> The fierce anger of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall not return, until he have done <hi type="italic">it,</hi> and until he have performed the intents of his heart: in the latter days ye shall consider it. <div eID="gen17858" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17859" type="x-p"/> We have here further intimations of the favour God had in reserve for them after the days of their calamity were over. It is promised, <div eID="gen17859" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17860" type="x-p"/> I. That the city and temple should be rebuilt, <reference osisRef="Jer.30.18">v. 18</reference>. <hi type="italic">Jacob's tents,</hi> and <hi type="italic">his dwelling places,</hi> felt the effects of <hi type="italic">the captivity,</hi> for they lay in ruins when the inhabitants were carried away captives; but, when they have returned, the habitations shall be repaired, and raised up out of their ruins, and therein God will <hi type="italic">have mercy upon their dwelling places,</hi> that had been monuments of his justice. Then <hi type="italic">the city</hi> of Jerusalem <hi type="italic">shall be built upon her own heap,</hi> her own hill, though now it be no better than a ruinous heap. The situation was unexceptionable, and therefore it shall be rebuilt upon the same spot of ground. He that can <hi type="italic">make of a city a heap</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.25.2">Isa. xxv. 2</reference>) can when he pleases <hi type="italic">make of a heap a city</hi> again. <hi type="italic">The palace</hi> (the temple, God's palace) <hi type="italic">shall remain after the manner thereof;</hi> it shall be built after the old model; and the service of God shall be constantly kept up there and attended as formerly. <div eID="gen17860" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17861" type="x-p"/> II. That the sacred feasts should again be solemnized (<reference osisRef="Jer.30.19">v. 19</reference>): <hi type="italic">Out of</hi> the city, and the temple, and all the dwelling-places of Jacob, <hi type="italic">shall proceed thanksgiving and the voice of those that make merry.</hi> They shall go with expressions of joy to the temple service, and with the like shall return from it. Observe, The voice of <hi type="italic">thanksgiving</hi> is the same with <hi type="italic">the voice of those that make merry;</hi> for whatever is the matter of our joy should be the matter of our praise. <hi type="italic">Is any merry? Let him sing psalms.</hi> What makes us cheerful should make us thankful. <hi type="italic">Serve the Lord with gladness.</hi> <div eID="gen17861" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17862" type="x-p"/> III. That the people should be multiplied, and increased, and made considerable: <hi type="italic">They shall not be few, they shall not be small,</hi> but shall become numerous and illustrious, and make a figure among the nations; for <hi type="italic">I will multiply them</hi> and <hi type="italic">I will glorify them.</hi> It is for the honour of the church to have many added to it that shall be saved. This would make them be of some weight among their neighbours. Let a people be ever so much diminished and despised, God can multiply and glorify them. They shall be restored to their former honour: <hi type="italic">Their children shall be as aforetime,</hi> playing in the streets (<reference osisRef="Zech.8.5">Zech. viii. 5</reference>); they shall inherit their parents' estates and honours as formerly; <hi type="italic">and their congregation shall,</hi> both in civil and sacred things, <hi type="italic">be established before me.</hi> There shall be a constant succession of faithful magistrates in the congregation of the elders, to establish that, and of faithful worshippers in the congregation of the saints. As one generation passes away another shall be raised up, and so the <hi type="italic">congregation shall be established before</hi> God. <div eID="gen17862" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17863" type="x-p"/> IV. That they shall be blessed with a good government (<reference osisRef="Jer.30.21">v. 21</reference>): <hi type="italic">Their nobles</hi> and judges <hi type="italic">shall be of themselves,</hi> of their own nation, and they shall no longer be ruled by strangers and enemies; <hi type="italic">their governor shall proceed from the midst of them,</hi> shall be one that has been a sharer with them in the afflictions of their captive state; and this has reference to Christ our <hi type="italic">governor, David our King</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.30.9">v. 9</reference>); he is of ourselves, <hi type="italic">in all things made like unto his brethren. And I will cause him to draw near;</hi> this may be understood either, 1. Of the people, Jacob and Israel: "<hi type="italic">I will cause</hi> them <hi type="italic">to draw near</hi> to me in the temple service, as formerly, to come in to covenant with me, as <hi type="italic">my people</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.30.22">v. 22</reference>), to <hi type="italic">approach to me</hi> in communion; <hi type="italic">for who</hi> hath <hi type="italic">engaged his heart,</hi> made a covenant with it, and brought it into bonds, <hi type="italic">to approach unto me?</hi>" How few are there that do so! None can do it but by the special grace of God <hi type="italic">causing them to draw near.</hi> Note, Whenever we approach to God in any holy ordinance we must engage our hearts to do it; the heart must be prepared for the duty, employed in it, and kept closely to it. The heart is the main thing that God looks at and requires; but it is deceitful, and will start aside of a great deal of care and pains be not taken to engage it, to bind this <hi type="italic">sacrifice with cords.</hi> Or, 2. It may be understood of the governor; for it is a single person that is spoken of: <hi type="italic">Their governor shall</hi> be duly called to his office, shall <hi type="italic">draw near</hi> to God to consult him upon all occasions. God <hi type="italic">will cause him to approach to</hi> him, for, otherwise, who would engage to take care of so weak a people, and let this ruin come under their hand? But when God has work to do, though attended with many discouragements, he will raise up instruments to do it. But it looks further, to Christ, to him as Mediator. Note, (1.) The proper work and office of Christ, as Mediator, is <hi type="italic">to draw near and approach unto</hi> God, not for himself only, but for us, and in our name and stead, as the high priest of our profession. The priests are said to draw nigh to God, <reference osisRef="Lev.10.3">Lev. x. 3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.21.17">xxi. 17</reference>. <hi type="italic">Moses drew near,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.20.21">Exod. xx. 21</reference>. (2.) God the Father did <hi type="italic">cause</hi> Jesus Christ thus <hi type="italic">to draw near and approach to</hi> him as Mediator. He commanded and appointed him to do it; he sanctified and sealed him, anointed him for this purpose, accepted him, and declared himself well pleased in him. (3.) Jesus Christ, being caused by the Father to approach unto him as Mediator, did <hi type="italic">engage his heart to</hi> do it, that is, he bound and obliged himself to it, <hi type="italic">undertook for his heart</hi> (so some read it), for his soul, that, in the fullness of time, it should be <hi type="italic">made an offering for sin.</hi> His own voluntary undertaking, in compliance with his Father's will and in compassion to fallen man, engaged him, and then his own honour kept him to it. It also intimates that he was hearty and resolute, free and cheerful, in it, and made nothing of the difficulties that lay in his way, <reference osisRef="Isa.63.3-Isa.63.5">Isa. lxiii. 3-5</reference>. (4.) Jesus Christ was, in all this, truly wonderful. We may well ask, with admiration, <hi type="italic">Who is this that</hi> thus <hi type="italic">engages his heart</hi> to such an undertaking? <div eID="gen17863" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17864" type="x-p"/> V. That they shall be taken again into covenant with God, according to the covenant made with their fathers (<reference osisRef="Jer.30.22">v. 22</reference>): <hi type="italic">You shall be my people;</hi> and it is God's good work in us that makes us <hi type="italic">to him a people, a people for his name,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.15.14">Acts xv. 14</reference>. <hi type="italic">I will be your God.</hi> It is his good-will to us that is the summary of that part of the covenant. <div eID="gen17864" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17865" type="x-p"/> VI. That their enemies shall be reckoned with and brought down (<reference osisRef="Jer.30.20">v. 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will punish all</hi> those <hi type="italic">that oppress them,</hi> so that it shall appear to all a dangerous thing to <hi type="italic">touch God's anointed,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.105.15">Ps. cv. 15</reference>. The <reference osisRef="Jer.30.23-Jer.30.24">last two verses</reference> come under this head: <hi type="italic">The whirlwind of the Lord shall fall with pain upon the head of the wicked.</hi> These two verses we had before (<reference osisRef="Jer.23.19-Jer.23.20">ch. xxiii. 19, 20</reference>); <hi type="italic">there</hi> they were a denunciation of God's wrath against the wicked hypocrites in Israel; <hi type="italic">here</hi> against the wicked oppressors of Israel. The expressions, exactly agreeing, speak the same with that (<reference osisRef="Isa.51.22-Isa.51.23">Isa. li. 22, 23</reference>), <hi type="italic">I will take the cup of trembling out of thy hand and put it into the hand of those that afflict thee.</hi> The wrath of God against the wicked is here represented to be. 1. Very terrible, like a whirlwind, surprising and irresistible. 2. Very grievous. It <hi type="italic">shall fall with pain upon their heads;</hi> they shall be as much hurt as frightened. 3. It shall pursue them. Whirlwinds are usually short, but this shall be <hi type="italic">a continuing whirlwind.</hi> 4. It shall accomplish that for which it is sent: <hi type="italic">The anger of the Lord shall not return till he have done it.</hi> The purposes of his wrath, as well as the purposes of his love, will all be fulfilled; he will <hi type="italic">perform the intents of his heart.</hi> 5. Those that will not lay this to heart now will then be unable to put off the thoughts of it: <hi type="italic">In the latter days you shall consider it,</hi> when it will be too late to prevent it.  <chapter eID="Jer.30"/> <div eID="gen17865" type="x-p"/>

entries.60a9d51df298b627224af0749dee978029e733f4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10230"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 30</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Jer.30.1-Jer.30.24">Jr 30:1-24</reference>. Restoration of the Jews from Babylon after Its Capture, and Raising Up of Messiah.</title> <div sID="gen18235" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10230"/><hi type="bold">2. Write ... in a book--</hi>After the destruction of Jerusalem Jeremiah is not ordered as heretofore to speak, but to write the succeeding prophecy (<reference osisRef="Jer.30.4">Jr 30:4</reference>, &c.), so as thereby it might be read by his countrymen wheresoever they might be in their dispersion. <div eID="gen18235" type="x-p"/>
entries.0588782d19f5c03d7237e484df269ca0eefada27: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10231"/><div sID="gen18236" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10231"/><hi type="bold">3. bring again ... captivity of ... Israel and Judah--</hi>the restoration not merely of the Jews (treated of in this thirtieth chapter), but also of the ten tribes ("Israel"; treated in the thirty-first chapter), together forming the whole nation (<reference osisRef="Jer.30.18">Jr 30:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.32.44">Jr 32:44</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.39.25">Eze 39:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.9.14">Am 9:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amos.9.15">15</reference>). "Israel" is mentioned first because its exile was longer than that of Judah. Some captives of the Israelite ten tribes returned with those of Judah (<reference osisRef="Luke.2.36">Lu 2:36</reference>; "Aser" is mentioned). But these are only a pledge of the full restoration hereafter (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.26">Ro 11:26</reference>, "All Israel"). Compare <reference osisRef="Jer.16.15">Jr 16:15</reference>. This third verse is a brief statement of the subject before the prophecy itself is given. <div eID="gen18236" type="x-p"/>
entries.4eb47a75a9073fb77ba8b41562747f037b8c88cd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10232"/><div sID="gen18237" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10232"/><hi type="bold">5. We have heard ... trembling--</hi>God introduces the Jews speaking that which they will be reduced to at last in spite of their stubbornness. Threat and promise are combined: the former briefly; namely, the misery of the Jews in the Babylonian captivity down to their "trembling" and "fear" arising from the approach of the Medo-Persian army of Cyrus against Babylon; the promise is more fully dwelt on; namely, their "trembling" will issue in a deliverance as speedy as is the transition from a woman's labor pangs to her joy at giving birth to a child (<reference osisRef="Jer.30.6">Jr 30:6</reference>). <div eID="gen18237" type="x-p"/>
entries.5ade76dead0cdcd9fcb57dcd8cadca117d72d91b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10233"/><div sID="gen18238" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10233"/><hi type="bold">6. Ask--</hi>Consult all the authorities, men or books, you can, you will not find an instance. Yet in that coming day men will be seen with their hands pressed on their loins, as women do to repress their pangs. God will drive men through pain to gestures more fitting a woman than a man (<reference osisRef="Jer.4.31">Jr 4:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.6.24">6:24</reference>). The metaphor is often used to express the previous pain followed by the sudden deliverance of Israel, as in the case of a woman in childbirth (<reference osisRef="Isa.66.7-Isa.66.9">Is 66:7-9</reference>).<div eID="gen18238" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18239" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">paleness--</hi>properly the color of herbs blasted and fading: the green paleness of one in jaundice: the sickly paleness of terror. <div eID="gen18239" type="x-p"/>
entries.fd2e6b03c1883e22fbe1a45d7bd29bf11f869a63: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10234"/><div sID="gen18240" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10234"/><hi type="bold">7. great--</hi>marked by great calamities (<reference osisRef="Joel.2.11">Joe 2:11</reference>, 31; <reference osisRef="Amos.5.18">Am 5:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zeph.1.14">Zep 1:14</reference>).<div eID="gen18240" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18241" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">none like it ... but he shall be saved--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Dan.12.1">Da 12:1</reference>). The partial deliverance at Babylon's downfall prefigures the final, complete deliverance of Israel, literal and spiritual, at the downfall of the mystical Babylon (<reference osisRef="Rev.18.1-Rev.19.21">Re 18:1-19:21</reference>). <div eID="gen18241" type="x-p"/>
entries.a6768cf704b42c8ff9c86ba208334e57b9f1a406: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10235"/><div sID="gen18242" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10235"/><hi type="bold">8. his yoke ... thy neck--</hi>his, that is, Jacob's (<reference osisRef="Jer.30.7">Jr 30:7</reference>), the yoke imposed on him. The transition to the second person is frequent, God speaking of Jacob or Israel, at the same time addressing him directly. So "him" rightly follows; "foreigners shall no more make him their servant" (<reference osisRef="Jer.25.14">Jr 25:14</reference>). After the deliverance by Cyrus, Persia, Alexander, Antiochus, and Rome made Judah their servant. The full of deliverance meant must, therefore, be still future. <div eID="gen18242" type="x-p"/>
entries.081b4f95b2d3076a15bf28c6a2902487e7a472b3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10236"/><div sID="gen18243" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10236"/>9. Instead of serving strangers (<reference osisRef="Jer.30.8">Jr 30:8</reference>), they shall serve the Lord, their rightful King in the theocracy (<reference osisRef="Ezek.21.27">Eze 21:27</reference>).<div eID="gen18243" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18244" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">David, their king--</hi>No king of David's seed has held the scepter since the captivity; for Zerubbabel, though of David's line, never claimed the title of "king." The Son of David, Messiah, must therefore be meant; so the Targum (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.55.3">Is 55:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.55.4">4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.23">Eze 34:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.24">24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.37.24">37:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.3.5">Ho 3:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.11.25-Rom.11.32">Ro 11:25-32</reference>). He was appointed to the throne of David (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.7">Is 9:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.1.32">Lu 1:32</reference>). He is here joined with Jehovah as claiming equal allegiance. God is our "King," only when we are subject to Christ; God rules us not immediately, but through His Son (<reference osisRef="John.5.22">Joh 5:22</reference>, 23, 27).<div eID="gen18244" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18245" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">raise up--</hi>applied to the judges whom God raised up as deliverers of Israel out of the hand of its oppressors (<reference osisRef="Judg.2.16">Jud 2:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.9">3:9</reference>). So Christ was raised up as the antitypical Deliverer (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.6">Psa 2:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.1.69">Lu 1:69</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.2.30">Ac 2:30</reference>; 13:23). <div eID="gen18245" type="x-p"/>
entries.c4d3b7211294c391f8a37024ca9c436e1b550a0a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10237"/><div sID="gen18246" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10237"/><hi type="bold">10. from afar--</hi>Be not afraid as if the distance of the places whither ye are to be dispersed precludes the possibility of return.<div eID="gen18246" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18247" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seed--</hi>Though through the many years of captivity intervening, you yourselves may not see the restoration, the promise shall be fulfilled to your seed, primarily at the return from Babylon, fully at the final restoration.<div eID="gen18247" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18248" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">quiet ... none ... make ... afraid--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.23.6">Jr 23:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.14.11">Zec 14:11</reference>). <div eID="gen18248" type="x-p"/>
entries.d761171db752296ce2a951df7dafe133730f4890: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10238"/><div sID="gen18249" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10238"/><hi type="bold">11. though ... full end of all nations ... yet ... not ... of thee--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Amos.9.8">Am 9:8</reference>). The punishment of reprobates is final and fatal; that of God's people temporary and corrective. Babylon was utterly destroyed: Israel after chastisement was delivered.<div eID="gen18249" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18250" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in measure--</hi>literally, "with judgment," that is, moderation, not in the full rigor of justice (<reference osisRef="Jer.10.24">Jr 10:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.46.28">46:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.6.1">Psa 6:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.27.8">Is 27:8</reference>).<div eID="gen18250" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18251" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not ... altogether unpunished--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Exod.34.7">Ex 34:7</reference>). <div eID="gen18251" type="x-p"/>
entries.d3d81b78de7ad37e853da138959719e422cfece8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10239"/><div sID="gen18252" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10239"/>12. The desperate circumstances of the Jews are here represented as an incurable wound. Their sin is so grievous that their hope of the punishment (their exile) soon coming to an end is vain (<reference osisRef="Jer.8.22">Jr 8:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.15.18">15:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.36.16">2Ch 36:16</reference>). <div eID="gen18252" type="x-p"/>
entries.b0fdd19437e4af85fca76631c872ae8155167f8c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10240"/><div sID="gen18253" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10240"/><hi type="bold">13. none to plead--</hi>a new image from a court of justice.<div eID="gen18253" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18254" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bound up--</hi>namely, with the bandages applied to tie up a wound.<div eID="gen18254" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18255" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">no healing medicines--</hi>literally, "medicines of healing," or else applications, (literally, "ascensions") of medicaments. <div eID="gen18255" type="x-p"/>
entries.6e3b191fd8b1cdc3b3ecc7fa1f941d4cc367d963: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10241"/><div sID="gen18256" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10241"/><hi type="bold">14. lovers--</hi>the peoples formerly allied to thee, Assyria and Egypt (compare <reference osisRef="Lam.1.2">La 1:2</reference>).<div eID="gen18256" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18257" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seek thee not--</hi>have cast away all concern for thee in thy distress.<div eID="gen18257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18258" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wound of an enemy--</hi>a wound such as an enemy would inflict. God condescends to employ language adapted to human conceptions. He is incapable of "enmity" or "cruelty"; it was their grievous sin which righteously demanded a grievous punishment, as though He were an "enemy" (<reference osisRef="Jer.5.6">Jr 5:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.13.24">Job 13:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.30.21">30:21</reference>). <div eID="gen18258" type="x-p"/>
entries.b6f21ce5c2188edbb61a6a091675474dd1ce908d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10242"/><div sID="gen18259" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10242"/><hi type="bold">15. Why criest thou--</hi>as if God's severity was excessive. Thou hast no reason to complain, for thine affliction is just. Thy cry is too late, for the time of repentance and mercy is past [Calvin]. <div eID="gen18259" type="x-p"/>
entries.85fadf9e5ff89294ca7ef7769aac9273d109f271: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10243"/><div sID="gen18260" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10243"/><hi type="bold">16. Therefore--</hi>connected with <reference osisRef="Jer.30.13">Jr 30:13</reference>, because "There is none to plead thy cause ... therefore" I will plead thy cause, and heal thy wound, by overwhelming thy foes. This fifteenth verse is inserted to amplify what was said at the close of <reference osisRef="Jer.30.14">Jr 30:14</reference>. When the false ways of peace, suggested by the so-called prophets, had only ended in the people's irremediable ruin, the true prophet comes forward to announce the grace of God as bestowing repentance and healing.<div eID="gen18260" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18261" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">devour thee ... be devoured ... spoil ... be a spoil ... prey upon ... give for a prey--</hi>retribution in kind (see on <reference osisRef="Jer.2.3">Jr 2:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.23.22">Ex 23:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.33.1">Is 33:1</reference>). <div eID="gen18261" type="x-p"/>
entries.bdc14a432e1778e0572d83e8489c82136f7da521: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10244"/><div sID="gen18262" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10244"/>17. (<reference osisRef="Jer.8.22">Jr 8:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.33.6">33:6</reference>).<div eID="gen18262" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18263" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Outcast--</hi>as a wife put away by her husband (<reference osisRef="Isa.62.4">Is 62:4</reference>, contrasted with <reference osisRef="Jer.30.12">Jr 30:12</reference>).<div eID="gen18263" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18264" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Zion--</hi>alluding to its Hebrew meaning, "dryness"; "sought after" by none, as would be the case with an arid region (<reference osisRef="Isa.62.12">Is 62:12</reference>). The extremity of the people, so far from being an obstacle to, will be the chosen opportunity of, God's grace. <div eID="gen18264" type="x-p"/>
entries.84ce24ec091cb4b8afb451b5a987d6ad32e2d203: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10245"/><div sID="gen18265" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10245"/><hi type="bold">18. bring again ... captivity--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.33.7">Jr 33:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.33.11">11</reference>).<div eID="gen18265" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18266" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">tents--</hi>used to intimate that their present dwellings in Chaldea were but temporary as tents.<div eID="gen18266" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18267" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">have mercy on dwelling-places--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.102.13">Psa 102:13</reference>).<div eID="gen18267" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18268" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">own heap--</hi>on the same hill, that is, site, a hill being the usual site chosen for a city (compare <reference osisRef="Josh.11.13">Jos 11:13</reference>, Margin). This better answers the parallel clause, "after the manner thereof" (that is, in the same becoming ways as formerly), than the rendering, "its own heap of ruins," as in <reference osisRef="Jer.49.2">Jr 49:2</reference>.<div eID="gen18268" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18269" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">palace--</hi>the king's, on Mount Zion.<div eID="gen18269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18270" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">remain--</hi>rather, "shall be inhabited" (see on <reference osisRef="Jer.17.6">Jr 17:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.17.25">Jr 17:25</reference>). This confirms English Version, "palace," not as others translate, "the temple" (see <reference osisRef="1Kgs.16.18">1Ki 16:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.25">2Ki 15:25</reference>). <div eID="gen18270" type="x-p"/>
entries.bbeff24f3b88ee3163d6b014c7d4e454e515694d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10246"/><div sID="gen18271" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10246"/><hi type="bold">19. thanksgiving--</hi>The Hebrew word includes confession as well as praise; for, in the case of God, the highest praises we can bestow are only confessing what God really is [Bengel], (<reference osisRef="Jer.17.26">Jr 17:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.31.12">31:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.13">13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.33.11">33:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.35.10">Is 35:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.51.11">51:11</reference>).<div eID="gen18271" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18272" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">multiply them--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Zech.10.8">Zec 10:8</reference>). <div eID="gen18272" type="x-p"/>
entries.942f33e6b1d182e8d210e6dc6fddfce1f95e9769: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10247"/><div sID="gen18273" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10247"/><hi type="bold">20. as aforetime--</hi>as flourishing as in the time of David. <div eID="gen18273" type="x-p"/>
entries.89e88f814ae2b1474a704ae73b19f685335e5d19: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10248"/><div sID="gen18274" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10248"/><hi type="bold">21. their nobles--</hi>rather, "their Glorious One," or "Leader" (compare <reference osisRef="Acts.3.15">Ac 3:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.2.10">He 2:10</reference>), answering to "their Governor" in the parallel clause.<div eID="gen18274" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18275" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of themselves--</hi>of their own nation, a Jew, not a foreigner; applicable to Zerubbabel, or J. Hyrcanus (hereditary high priest and governor), only as types of Christ (<reference osisRef="Gen.49.10">Ge 49:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.5.2">Mi 5:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.9.5">Ro 9:5</reference>), the antitypical "David" (<reference osisRef="Jer.30.9">Jr 30:9</reference>).<div eID="gen18275" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18276" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cause him to draw near--</hi>as the great Priest (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.22">Ex 19:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.21.17">Le 21:17</reference>), through whom believers also have access to God (<reference osisRef="Heb.10.19-Heb.10.22">He 10:19-22</reference>). His priestly and kingly characters are similarly combined (<reference osisRef="Ps.110.4">Psa 110:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.6.13">Zec 6:13</reference>).<div eID="gen18276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18277" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">who ... engaged ... heart to approach--</hi>literally, "pledged his heart," that is, his life; a thing unique; Messiah alone has made His life responsible as the surety (<reference osisRef="Heb.7.22">He 7:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.9.11-Heb.9.15">9:11-15</reference>), in order to gain access not only for Himself, but for us to God. Heart is here used for life, to express the courage which it needed to undertake such a tremendous suretyship. The question implies admiration at one being found competent by His twofold nature, as God and man, for the task. Compare the interrogation (<reference osisRef="Isa.63.1-Isa.63.3">Is 63:1-3</reference>). <div eID="gen18277" type="x-p"/>
entries.83720b167885b2af9bb6a7618d5889b33abf94e2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10249"/><div sID="gen18278" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10249"/><hi type="bold">22. ye shall be my people, &c.--</hi>The covenant shall be renewed between God and His people through Messiah's mediation (<reference osisRef="Jer.30.21">Jr 30:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.31.1">31:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.33">33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.32.38">32:38</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.11.20">Eze 11:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.28">36:28</reference>). <div eID="gen18278" type="x-p"/>
entries.d6366f9b61e8990fa796be4fd986af318708eb8b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10250"/><div sID="gen18279" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10250"/>23-24. (<reference osisRef="Jer.23.19">Jr 23:19</reference>). Vengeance upon God's foes always accompanies manifestations of His grace to His people.<div eID="gen18279" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18280" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">continuing--</hi>literally, "sojourning," abiding constantly; appropriately here in the case of Babylon, which was to be permanently destroyed, substituted for "whirling itself about" ("grievous" in English Version) (see on <reference osisRef="Jer.23.19">Jr 23:19</reference>,<reference osisRef="Jer.23.20">20</reference>), where the temporary downfall of Judea is spoken of. <chapter eID="Jer.30"/>

entries.928218b091813f4294f543517e16c056f628c664: <div eID="gen30076" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen30077" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen30078" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen30078" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen30077" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen30079" type="x-p"/> This and the following chapter must relate to a still future restoration of the posterity of Jacob from their several dispersions, as no deliverance hitherto afforded them comes up to the terms of it; for, after the return from Babylon, they were again enslaved by the Greeks and Romans, contrary to the prediction in the eighth verse; in every papistical country they have labored under great civil disabilities, and in some of them have been horribly persecuted; upon the ancient people has this mystic Babylon very heavily laid her yoke; and in no place in the world are they at present their own masters; so that this prophecy remains to be fulfilled in the reign of David, i.e., the Messiah; the type, according to the general structure of the prophetical writings, being put for the antitype. The prophecy opens by an easy transition from the temporal deliverance spoken of before, and describes the mighty revolutions that shall precede the restoration of the descendants of Israel, <reference osisRef="Jer.30.1-Jer.30.9">Jer 30:1-9</reference>, who are encouraged to trust in the promises of God, <reference osisRef="Jer.30.10">Jer 30:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.30.11">Jer 30:11</reference>. They are, however, to expect corrections; which shall have a happy issue in future period, <reference osisRef="Jer.30.12-Jer.30.17">Jer 30:12-17</reference>. The great blessings of Messiah's reign are enumerated, <reference osisRef="Jer.30.18-Jer.30.22">Jer 30:18-22</reference>; and the wicked and impenitent declared to have no share in them, <reference osisRef="Jer.30.23">Jer 30:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.30.24">Jer 30:24</reference>. <div eID="gen30079" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30080" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen30080" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30081" type="x-p"/> The word that came to Jeremiah from the Lord - This prophecy was delivered about a year after the taking of Jerusalem; so Dahler. Dr. Blayney supposes it and the following chapter to refer to the future restoration of both Jews and Israelites in the times of the Gospel; though also touching at the restoration from the Babylonish captivity, at the end of seventy years. Supposing these two chapters to be penned after the taking of Jerusalem, which appears the most natural, they will refer to the same events, one captivity shadowing forth another, and one restoration being the type or pledge of the second.
entries.8a6dab16a6296d412fdcec05236782393e2211c1: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen30081" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30082" type="x-p"/> Write thee all the words that I have spoken unto thee in a book - The book here recommended I believe to be the thirtieth and thirty-first chapters; for among the Hebrews any portion of writing, in which the subject was finished, however small, was termed ספר sepher, a Book, a treatise or discourse.
entries.066985d7df77749f3a2b6f977c291466aea4ed92: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen30082" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30083" type="x-p"/> The days come - First, After the conclusion of the seventy years. Secondly, Under the Messiah. <div eID="gen30083" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30084" type="x-p"/> That I will bring again the captivity of Israel - The ten tribes, led captive by the king of Assyria, and dispersed among the nations. <div eID="gen30084" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30085" type="x-p"/> And Judah - The people carried into Babylon at two different times; first, under Jeconiah, and, secondly, under Zedekiah, by Nebuchadnezzar.
entries.57d0251884baa737b78b949aa3296738c8cf59d0: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen30085" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30086" type="x-p"/> We have heard a voice of trembling - This may refer to the state and feelings of the people during the war which Cyrus carried on against the Babylonians. Trembling and terror would no doubt affect them, and put an end to peace and all prosperity; as they could not tell what would be the issue of the struggle, and whether their state would be better or worse should their present masters fall in the conflict. This is well described in the next verse, where men are represented as being, through pain and anguish, like women in travail. See the same comparison <reference osisRef="Isa.13.6-Isa.13.8">Isa 13:6-8</reference>.
entries.28099c37bba69f22c492c27d4702f5e4f5393040: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen30086" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30087" type="x-p"/> Alas! for that day is great - When the Medes and Persians with all their forces shall come on the Chaldeans, it will be the day of Jacob's trouble - trial, dismay, and uncertainty; but he shall be delivered out of it - the Chaldean empire shall fall, but the Jews shall be delivered by Cyrus. Jerusalem shall be destroyed by the Romans, but the Israel of God shall be delivered from its ruin. Not one that had embraced Christianity perished in the sackage of that city.
entries.ed89666f0f86e87eef74bd8cbeb84fa56b1f6253: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen30087" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30088" type="x-p"/> I will break his yoke - That is, the yoke of Nebuchadnezzar. <div eID="gen30088" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30089" type="x-p"/> Of him - Of Jacob, (<reference osisRef="Jer.30.7">Jer 30:7</reference>), viz., the then captive Jews.
entries.7dce470156a23c98d1912691d86d3af7d85ffdb6: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen30089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30090" type="x-p"/> But they shall serve the Lord their God, and David their King - This must refer to the times of the Messiah and hence the Chaldee has, "They shall obey the Lord their God, וישת מאון למשיחה בר דוד veyishta meun limschicha bar David, and they shall obey the Messiah, the Son of David." This is a very remarkable version; and shows that it was a version, not according to the letter, but according to their doctrine and their expectation. David was long since dead; and none of his descendants ever reigned over them after the Babylonish captivity, nor have they since been a regal nation. Zerubbabel, under the Persians, and the Asmoneans, can be no exception to this. They have been no nation since; they are no nation now; and it is only in the latter days that they can expect to be a nation, and that must be a Christian nation. <div eID="gen30090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30091" type="x-p"/> Christ is promised under the name of his progenitor, David, <reference osisRef="Isa.55.3">Isa 55:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.55.4">Isa 55:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eze.34.23">Eze 34:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eze.34.24">Eze 34:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eze.37.24">Eze 37:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eze.37.25">Eze 37:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.3.5">Hos 3:5</reference>.
entries.590657b8fdfbf17dfac333ae0a2cc796264f5815: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen30091" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30092" type="x-p"/> Though I make a full end of all nations - Though the Persians destroy the nations whom they vanquish, yet they shall not destroy thee.
entries.30dd314afe5dee15b057d31bea8f0428d325d070: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen30092" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30093" type="x-p"/> Thy bruise is incurable - אנוש anush, desperate, not incurable; for the cure is promised in <reference osisRef="Jer.30.17">Jer 30:17</reference>, I will restore health unto thee, and I will heal thee of thy wounds.
entries.f22d06b42cc1d95c997abb13697283ad8f7573f7: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen30093" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30094" type="x-p"/> There is none to plead thy cause - All thy friends and allies have forsaken thee.
entries.a95bedb660693e9b32dd87c3686c01d6aea30035: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen30094" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30095" type="x-p"/> Thy sorrow is incurable - אנוש anush, desperate. See <reference osisRef="Jer.30.12">Jer 30:12</reference>.
entries.2b920fa4bf4c1ed7fca1e2d49e115b118ad89a96: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen30095" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30096" type="x-p"/> They that devour thee - The Chaldeans. <div eID="gen30096" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30097" type="x-p"/> Shall be devoured - By the Medes and Persians. <div eID="gen30097" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30098" type="x-p"/> All that prey upon thee will I give for a prey - The Assyrians were destroyed by the Babylonians; the Babylonians, by the Medes and Persians; the Egyptians and Persians were destroyed by the Greeks, under Alexander. All these nations are now extinct, but the Jews, as a distinct people, still exist.
entries.8559ba796d94466766f44bc524ea06f5264bca6e: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen30098" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30099" type="x-p"/> The city shall be builded upon her own heap - Be re-edified from its own ruins. See the book of Nehemiah, passim. <div eID="gen30099" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30100" type="x-p"/> And the palace shall remain - Meaning, the king's house shall be restored; or, more probably, the temple shall be rebuilt; which was true, for after the Babylonish captivity it was rebuilt by Nehemiah, etc. By the tents, distinguished from the dwelling-places of Jacob, we may understand all the minor dispersions of the Jews, as well as those numerous synagogues found in large cities.
entries.f16fb63e508c520d33b3d7659b1b04b0cce1f257: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen30100" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30101" type="x-p"/> I will multiply them - They shall be very numerous; even where at present they have but tents. <div eID="gen30101" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30102" type="x-p"/> I will also glorify them - I will put honor upon them every where, so that they shall be no longer contemptible. This will be a very great change, for they are now despised all over the earth.
entries.96af97ba43b4db4ccaab132e7fde4974647c8967: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen30102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30103" type="x-p"/> Their children also - They shall have the education of their own children as formerly. <div eID="gen30103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30104" type="x-p"/> And their congregation - Their religious assemblies. <div eID="gen30104" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30105" type="x-p"/> Shall be established - Being, in the latter days, incorporated with those "who serve the Lord their God, and worship the Messiah, the son of David."
entries.4d2f98c14222de5ea092d751fcb9072a48676657: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen30105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30106" type="x-p"/> Their nobles shall be of themselves - Strangers shall not rule over them; and - <div eID="gen30106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30107" type="x-p"/> Their governor shall proceed from the midst of them - Both Nehemiah and Zerubbabel, their nobles and governors after the return from Babylon, were Jews.
entries.7fb439c7957b6bdaf689a7332a545b15393f9efc: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen30107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30108" type="x-p"/> Ye shall be my people - The old covenant shall be renewed.
entries.f0abc6a08ea6e0bdf865b4ad1c0bc597c6388a20: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen30108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30109" type="x-p"/> The whirlwind of the Lord - A grievous tempest of desolation, - <div eID="gen30109" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30110" type="x-p"/> Shall fall with pain upon the head of the wicked - On Nebuchadnezzar and the Chaldeans.
entries.de10055b550ebe2e44b7d238562efddcfe57c23e: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen30110" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30111" type="x-p"/> In the latter days ye shall consider it - By the latter days the Gospel dispensation is generally meant; and that restoration which is the principal topic in this and the succeeding chapter refers to this time. Had the Jews properly considered this subject, they would long ere this have been brought into the liberty of the Gospel, and saved from the maledictions under which they now groan. Why do not the Jews read their own prophets more conscientiously?  <chapter eID="Jer.30"/> <div eID="gen30111" type="x-p"/>

entries.66a71bb483bf79d6a390dbe263a127b098f50bb8: <div eID="gen14179" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">B. The Announcement of Deliverance for All Israel - Jeremiah 30-33</title> <div sID="gen14180" type="x-p"/> In view of the impending fall of the kingdom of Judah, Jeremiah seeks to present the godly with a strong anchor of hope in the realization of God’s gracious promises, which were to be fulfilled after the appointed season of punishment had passed. For this purpose, after predicting the ills of exile times, the prophet gives a comprehensive statement concerning the deliverance which the Lord will vouchsafe to His people in the future, and gathers together the repeated briefer promises regarding the restoration and glorious condition of Israel and Judah, so as to give a full description of the deliverance intended for all the covenant people under the sceptre of the future David. This detailed announcement of the deliverance consists of a pretty long prophetic address (which Hengstenberg very properly designates "the triumphal hymn of Israel’s salvation," Jer 30 and 31), and two pieces confirmatory of this address, viz.: (1) one recording a symbolical act performed by the prophet at God’s command - the sale of a piece of hereditary property in land during the last siege of Jerusalem, shortly before the breaking up of the kingdom, which commenced with the taking of the city - together with a message from God explaining this act, Jer 32; ; and (2) another passage giving, in prophetic language, a renewed promise that Jerusalem and Judah would be restored with the blissful arrangements connected with the Davidic monarchy and the Levitical priesthood, Jer 33. According to the headings given in <reference osisRef="Jer.32.1">Jer 32:1</reference> and <reference osisRef="Jer.33.1">Jer 33:1</reference>, these two latter pieces belong to the tenth year of Zedekiah’s reign; the address contained in Jer 30 and 31, on the other hand, belongs to a somewhat earlier period, and was not uttered publicly before the people, but simply composed in writing, and meant to be preserved for future use. As regards the exact time of its composition, the views of modern expositors are very dissimilar. While Hengstenberg, with many others, places it in the same period with the allied chapters 32 and 33, viz., in the time when Jerusalem was being besieged, immediately before the capture and destruction of the city, Nägelsbach reckons this address among the oldest portions of the whole book, and assigns its composition to the times of King Josiah, to which <reference osisRef="Jer.3.11-Jer.3.25">Jer 3:11-25</reference> belongs. But the arguments adduced in support of this view are quite insufficient to establish it. It does not by any means follow from the substantial agreement of the address with that in Jer 3, so far as it exists, that they were both composed at the same time; and if (as Nägelsbach thinks) the fact that there is no mention made of the Chaldeans were taken as a criterion of composition before the fourth year of Jehoiakim, then, too, would the address in Jer 33 be put down as having been composed before that year, but in glaring contradiction to the inscription given Jer 33:1. And as little reason is there for inferring, with Hengstenberg, from <reference osisRef="Jer.30.5-Jer.30.7">Jer 30:5-7</reference>, that the final catastrophe of Jeremiah’s time is represented as still imminent; for these verses do not refer at all to the destruction of Jerusalem by the Chaldeans. That learned writer is, however, quite correct in his remark, that the prophet takes his stand-point within the period of the catastrophe, as if it had already begun, but that this time is an ideal present, so that we must not allow ourselves to be deceived as to the time of composition by the circumstance that, generally, Judah no less than Israel appears to be already in a state of exile, far from the land of the Lord. The time of composition cannot be made out with perfect certainty. Yet there is nothing against the assumption that it is the tenth year of Zedekiah. <div eID="gen14180" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Israel’s Deliverance and Glorious Condition in the Future - Jeremiah 30-31</title> <div sID="gen14181" type="x-p"/> A great day of judgment, before which all the world trembles, will bring to Israel deliverance from the yoke imposed on them. The Lord will bring them out of the land of their captivity (<reference osisRef="Jer.30.4-Jer.30.11">Jer 30:4-11</reference>). He will bind up and heal the wounds which He inflicted on them because of their sins; will render to those who oppressed and chastised them according to their deeds (<reference osisRef="Jer.30.12-Jer.30.17">Jer 30:12-17</reference>); will again build up His kingdom, and render His people glorious, both in temporal and spiritual respects (<reference osisRef="Jer.30.18-Jer.30.22">Jer 30:18-22</reference>). The wrath of the Lord will be poured forth upon all evil-doers like a tempest, till He has performed the thoughts of His heart at the end of the days (<reference osisRef="Jer.30.23">Jer 30:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.30.24">Jer 30:24</reference>).
