               <ns0:p n="10">10 ¶ Therefore <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Isa. 41.13. & 43.5. & 44.2. chap. 46.28.</ns0:note> fear thou not, O my ser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vant Jacob <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">You that are my servants, and the posterity of <ns0:hi>Iacob,</ns0:hi> though your Captivity be threescore and ten years, yet be not afraid that I have quite forgotten you, or my promise made to your Fathers.</ns0:note>, saith the LORD, neither be dis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mayed, O Israel; for lo, I will save thee from afar, and thy seed from the land of their captivity <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">For I will assure you that though I have for your sins sent you afar off, yet you are not be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />yond the reach of my saving Arm.</ns0:note>, and Jacob shall return, and shall be in rest and quiet, and none shall make <ns0:hi>him</ns0:hi> a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fraid <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">You shall return our of the Captivity of <ns0:hi>Babylon,</ns0:hi> and be at rest, as they were for 150 years during the time of the <ns0:hi>Persian Monarchy.</ns0:hi> A short History of which we have in the Books of <ns0:hi>Ezra</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Nehe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />miah.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="11">11 For I <ns0:hi>am</ns0:hi> with thee saith the LORD; to save thee <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">To save thee, with a Temporal Salvation, and deliverance, and those of thee who are <ns0:hi>Israelites</ns0:hi> indeed with a spiritual, and eternal Salvation, but the first is, what is here principally intended.</ns0:note>: <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Amos 9.8.</ns0:note> though I make a full end of all nations whither I have scattered thee, yet will I not make a full end of thee <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">God puts a difference betwixt the chastisements of his People, and the punishment of their Enemies, the latter he destroyeth with an utter, and total destruction, to make an end of them, but he chastens his People like a father for their profit, and will not bring them to utter ruine.</ns0:note>: but I will cor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rect thee <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 6.1. chap. 10.24. & 46.28.</ns0:note> in measure <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">He cor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rects them in measure; the <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> word signifieth in judg<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment; that is, not in Equity onely, but in Wisdom, or with Moderation, whereas he is said to punish his Enemies in fu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry. There are many Texts of Scripture that mention this difference which God puts betwixt his punishing his people, and his punishing their Enemies, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 26.14, 19. & 27.7, 8.</ns0:note>, and will not leave thee altogether unpunished <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">But yet God will not let his own people go altogether unpu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nished, that by it they may be reclaimed, and the World may take notice that God is of purer eyes than that he can in any persons behold iniquity.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">12 For thus saith the LORD, Thy <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 15.18.</ns0:note> bruise <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> incurable, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> thy wound <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> grievous <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Interpreters generally understand by <ns0:hi>bruise</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>wound</ns0:hi> here, the state that the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> should be in, in the Captivity of <ns0:hi>Ba<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bylon,</ns0:hi> which would be miserable and so miserable that it would be incurable from any hand except the hand of God, but I do not understand why it may not as well be interpreted of their <ns0:hi>sinful state,</ns0:hi> with reference to Gods purpose, and interpreted by 2 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 36.16. where it is said <ns0:hi>the wrath of God arose against them till there was no remedy.</ns0:hi> They had sinned to that degree that God had resolved into Captivity they should go, and there should abide till the determination of 70 years.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="13">13 <ns0:hi>There is</ns0:hi> none to plead thy cause <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>for bind<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing up or pres<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sing.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> that thou mayest be bound up: <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 8.22.</ns0:note> thou hast no heal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing medicines <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Concerning the general design of the Prophet in these words, all Interpreters seem agreed that the Prophets Scope is to bring their uneasie thoughts to a rest, and make them rest satisfied with the Providence of God, for there was no resistance of the Will of God which he metaphorically expresseth under the notion of one miserably and incurably wounded, whom no Physitian or Chirurgion could heal, and for whom there was no effectual Plaister, but concerning the particular sense of the <ns0:hi>Hebrew words,</ns0:hi> much is critically said, which I conceive not my work to repea<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, nor is it of much moment to us to know, whe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther the word more properly signifies <ns0:hi>healing medicines,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>courses of care,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>plaisters</ns0:hi>; those who are curious may read suffi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ciently about it in the <ns0:hi>English Annotations</ns0:hi> upon the Text. It may be more material to consider whether the Prophets mean<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing be, there was none would do it, or there was none could do it, or there was none should do it, that is, whom God would admit at present to do it, as he elsewhere saith, though <ns0:hi>Noah, Daniel</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Iob,</ns0:hi> and though <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Samuel</ns0:hi> stood before him, they should save none but their own Souls; the Prophets design doubtless was to satisfie this people, that there was no pres<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>nt remedy for them but Patience, though some would in charity plead for them, and though their false Prophets might promise a cure, yet in very deed God would admit now of no plea for them, and all means that could be used for their more speedy restauration, would proven no healing medicines, but like medicines that make the Patients worse, and irritate, instead of allaying the distemper.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="14">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:40" />14 All thy lovers have forgotten thee <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">In the time of thy prosperity thou hadst many friends, but now they have forgotten thee, very probably the <ns0:hi>Egyptians</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Assyrians,</ns0:hi> whose help the <ns0:hi>Iewes</ns0:hi> made often use of, are the lo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vers here intended, 2 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 28.21. <ns0:hi>Hos.</ns0:hi> 12.1. indeed the <ns0:hi>Egyptians</ns0:hi> were before conquered, or very much brought low, by the King of <ns0:hi>Babylon.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>: they seek thee not, for I have wounded thee with the wound <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Job 13.24. and 16.9. and 19.11.</ns0:note> of an enemy, with the chastisement of a <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Job 30.21.</ns0:note> cruel one <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">They see the miserable case they are in, and now do not covet thee as formerly, they discern that I have wounded thee with such a wound, as cruel men use to give their enemies.</ns0:note>, for the multitude of thine iniqui<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ty, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 5.6.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:hi>because</ns0:hi> thy sins were increased <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Though it be in me no act of cruelty, for it is but in a just punishment of your iniquities, which were increased to a very great multitude.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="15">15 Why criest thou for thine affliction? thy sorrow <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> incurable <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Why complainest thou of my dealings with thee? or as <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 15.18. The cause of thy sorrow is incurable, or as o<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, why complainest thou that thy sorrow <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>is incurable.</ns0:note>, for the multitude of thine iniquity: <ns0:hi>because</ns0:hi> thy sins were increased, I have done these things unto thee <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Though it be so, yet thou hast no reason to complain of my dealings, for thy destruction is of thy self; I am just in what I have done, for I have but given thee that death which is the wages of thy work of sin, nor was I suddenly provoked, it is for the multitude of thine iniquities, and in that case the living man hath no just reason to complain, <ns0:hi>Lam.</ns0:hi> 3.39.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="16">16 Therefore <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">The particle <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> is thought here to be ill Translated <ns0:hi>therefore,</ns0:hi> for manifestly it is not a causal or illative, and those who interpret it <ns0:hi>therefore,</ns0:hi> referr it to what went before, <ns0:hi>verse</ns0:hi> 10.11. It were better Translated <ns0:hi>nevertheless,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>notwithstanding yet,</ns0:hi> so the learned Author of the <ns0:hi>English Annotations</ns0:hi> thinks it should be Translated, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 7.14. and 30.18. and in many other Texts.</ns0:note> all they that devour thee <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Exod. 23.22.</ns0:note> shall be devoured, and all thine adversaries, every one of them shall go into captivity, and they that spoil thee shall be a spoil, and all that prey upon thee will I give for a prey <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">So this Text is a declaration of Gods free mercy, though this people had justly provoked the Lord by their iniquities to punish them, yet he would at length revenge them of their enemies, and those that spoiled them should feel his justice, and be themselves spoiled, so <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 10.12. and 33.1. God ordinarily punisheth those that have been ene<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mies to his people, more severely then his people have been punished by them, the reasons are, because though they serve God in chastising his people, yet they do it not designedly; <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 10.7. and commonly they exceed a measure in their exe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cuting Gods vengeance.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="17">17 For I will restore health <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">As the miserable state of this people was by the Prophet <ns0:hi>verse</ns0:hi> 12.13. described under the similitude of a man wound<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed, and bruised, and sick, so their more prosperous state is de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />scribed under the notion of health, and Gods action in restoring them, exprest under the notion of healing, both here, and in many other Texts, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 6.10. and 19.22. and 57.18, 19.</ns0:note> unto thee, and I will heal thee of thy wounds, saith the LORD, because they called thee an Outcast, <ns0:hi>saying,</ns0:hi> This <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> Zion, whom no man seeketh after <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">The particle here Translated <ns0:hi>because</ns0:hi> may so signifie here, for often the scorn and contempt of Gods peoples enemies, causeth God to make haste to their salvation, and deliverance, but many think that it were better Translated <ns0:hi>although,</ns0:hi> as it is, <ns0:hi>Ios.</ns0:hi> 17.18. though the Heathens call thee one that I have cast off, as a man doth his Wife; yet they shall see the contrary, for I will heal thee of thy wounds,</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Though they deriding say, this <ns0:hi>Zion</ns0:hi> whom none cares for: Some think that in this they alluded to the original signification of the word <ns0:hi>Tzion,</ns0:hi> which is a dry or wast place.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="18">18 ¶ Thus saith the LORD, Behold, I will bring again the captivity of Jacobs tents, and have mercy on his dwelling places <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">This verse manifestly is a promise of the rebuilding of the City, and was fulfilled in the times of <ns0:hi>Ezra,</ns0:hi> and the term <ns0:hi>cap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tivity,</ns0:hi> which in its proper sense relates to persons, not to pla<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ces, being here applyed to places, signifies the miserable state of <ns0:hi>Ierusalem,</ns0:hi> upon the taking it by <ns0:hi>Nebuchadnezzar,</ns0:hi> which God promiseth to change or alter under the notion of <ns0:hi>bringing again</ns0:hi>: So we read of the captivity of <ns0:hi>Iob,</ns0:hi> who yet strictly was never a captive, <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 42.10.</ns0:note>, and the ci<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ty shall be builded upon her own <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>little hill.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> heap, and the place shall remain after the manner there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />of <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Whether by the term <ns0:hi>heap</ns0:hi> be meant the heap of rubbish, into which the City was turned upon the taking of it by the King of <ns0:hi>Babylon,</ns0:hi> or the <ns0:hi>hill</ns0:hi> upon which the City was builded, is not much material; by the <ns0:hi>Pa<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ace</ns0:hi> is meant either the Kings house, or the Temple; So the verse is a pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mise of the building again of the City, the Temple, and the chief Governours house, all which was fulfilled by <ns0:hi>Ezra, Nehe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />miah</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Zorobabel,</ns0:hi> the History of which we read in the books wrote by <ns0:hi>Ezra</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Nehemiah.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="19">19 And <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Isa. 35.10. and 51.11.</ns0:note> out of them shall proceed thanks<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />giving <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Thanksgiving to God, as <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 17.26. either thank<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />offerings, <ns0:hi>Lev.</ns0:hi> 7.12, 13. or vocal Thanksgivings.</ns0:note>, and the voice of them that make mer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Ei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther in a religious sense, or in a civil sense, if it be taken in the former<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> it signifieth their mirth at their Religious Festi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vals, of which we read much in Scripture, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 42.4. and 118.15. <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> if in the latter, it signifieth their happy and joyful state after their restauration.</ns0:note>, and I will multiply them, and they shall not be few <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Though they be dimi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nished in the captivity, yet I will return to them in my wont<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed providences, and multiply them according to my promise to <ns0:hi>Abraham,</ns0:hi> so as they shall be for number <ns0:hi>many.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>; I will also glorifie them <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Ei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther in a religious sense, or in a civil sense, if it be taken in the former<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> it signifieth their mirth at their Religious Festi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vals, of which we read much in Scripture, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 42.4. and 118.15. <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> if in the latter, it signifieth their happy and joyful state after their restauration.</ns0:note>, and they shall not be small <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">And as to their quality it shall be honourable, though during those 70 years they shall be a people of mean, and no reputation, yet after that time they shall recover their ancient reputation, and again be a people great for honour and glory.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="20">20 Their children also shall be as aforetime <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Their posterity also shall be as happy, and in as much re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pute, as they were before this carrying into <ns0:hi>Babylon.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, and their congregation shall be established be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore me <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Their Church, or the body of the people of the <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> shall from Ge<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />neration to Generation be established.</ns0:note>, and I will punish all that oppress them <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">And though in those times there will be some that will oppress them, yet they shall not escape my vengeance that do it, for I will protect and de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fend them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="21">21 And their nobles shall be of themselves, and their governour shall proceed from the midst of them <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">This promise was made good in <ns0:hi>Zorobabel,</ns0:hi> and other Go<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vernours of the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> after their return out of captivity, till they came to be subdued by the <ns0:hi>Romans.</ns0:hi> Some restrain this unto Christ, and make it a prophesie of Christ, being born of the Jewish Nation, it is he they say that was meant by <ns0:hi>David, verse</ns0:hi> 9. and it is not improbable that the sense of the Text may reach unto Christ, but it seems literally to be understood of <ns0:hi>Zorobabel,</ns0:hi> and to be opposed to <ns0:hi>strangers</ns0:hi> ruling over them, which was no small piece of their calamity, while they were in captivity.</ns0:note>, and I will cause him to draw near, and he shall approach unto me <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">That is he shall serve me, and I will favour him, or this people shall serve me, and I will favour them, and not be as one at distance, or far off from them. Some understand this of the civil Governour that should be after the Captivity, some understand it of the people, some understand it of Christ; those that understand it of the Governour, make it to signifie the special favour that Governour should be in with God, and his Religion. Those that understand it of the people, make it to signifie the Religion of the people, and the favour they should be in with God. Those who understand it of Christ, in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />terpret it of his favour with God, by whom also the Saints have their access.</ns0:note>: for who <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> this that engaged his heart to approach unto me? saith the LORD <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Interpreters are yet more divided about this phrase; some apply it to Christ, either as an admiration of his excellency, or as denoting that none but he could draw near to God in that manner as he did, nor had any such a delight in the sons of men as he; so as for him to be a Me<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />diator betwixt offenders, and an offended God: None but he durst look in the face of an Angry God. Others understand it of <ns0:hi>Gods</ns0:hi> people intimating that in the day when they should return out of Captivity there would be but few, that with any serious purpose of heart would apply themselves unto God, or signify<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing the impotency that is in man heartily to draw nigh to God, till (as it is before said) God causeth him so to do; and some think the words have a reference to the Covenant mentioned in the next verse.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="22">
